title: A Study of Misinformation in Audio Messages Shared in WhatsApp Groups
screen_reason: No quantitative share of misinformation with a denominator is reported anywhere in the paper, and none is validly derivable. The corpus (42,869 audio messages, 16,503 unique audios, 11,700 with usable transcriptions) was never classified in full: misinformation was identified by TF-IDF cosine-similarity matching against a Brazilian fact-check claim database, after which ONLY the 300 highest-similarity pairs were manually inspected, of which 100 were confirmed. Everything else was labelled 'unchecked', and the authors state explicitly that 'strictly speaking, they might or might not carry misinformation'. The paper is a comparative content and propagation analysis of that fact-check-matched set against unchecked audios (topics, LIWC attributes, listener perceptions, lifetime, inter-share time, reach), not a prevalence study.
missed_or_uncertain: 1) DERIVABLE BUT REJECTED, flagged for the adjudicator: 100 unique audios were confirmed as carrying previously fact-checked false claims, and the analysis corpus is 11,700 unique transcribed audios (71% of 16,503 unique audios; 42,869 audio messages in 364 groups over six months). 100/11,700 = 0.85% would be an exact part/whole share of verbatim counts, but I did NOT create a row because the denominator was never classified: only the top 300 candidate pairs by cosine similarity were checked by hand, so the numerator is a function of an arbitrary candidate cutoff and is a lower bound of unquantifiable slack, not a prevalence estimate. 2) A further internal inconsistency argues against deriving anything: the Introduction says 'we marked over 120 unique audios that were shared more than 2,000 times across 260 groups during the monitored period', while Section 3.2 says 'only 100 out of the 300 transcriptions analyzed indeed carried the same content as the claim they were matched to ... These audios were marked as containing misinformation'. 100 vs 'over 120' cannot be reconciled from the text, and the share figure ('more than 2,000 times' out of 42,869 messages, i.e. roughly 4.7%) is stated only approximately. 3) NOT eligible: volunteer-survey figures, which are all computed INSIDE the misinformation-only or unchecked-only sets and are about perception, not veracity - volunteers judged audios with misinformation to be false 76% of the time (a discernment measure, explicitly out of scope); 58% of misinformation audios vs 17% of unchecked audios were reported as citing a source; a call to action was reported in 72% of misinformation audios vs 32% of unchecked; 9% vs 5% said they would share the audio (a hypothetical sharing INTENTION, explicitly out of scope); friendliness 1.78 vs 2.34 and naturality 1.65 vs 2.56 are scale means. 4) NOT eligible: LDA topic composition inside the misinformation set (52% of misinformation audios in topics 4 and 5; 18% in topic 7; 21% of unchecked audios in topic 2) - a topical breakdown of an all-misinformation set, not a veracity share. 5) NOT eligible as CONCENTRATION (fails R1): the propagation distributions ('20% of them were shared more than 13 times'; '90% of audios with misinformation are shared in at least 27 different groups'; '80% of audios with misinformation are shared by at least 12 different users') describe the distribution of shares across misinformation audios, not a top group of users or sources accounting for a stated share of exposure or sharing. 6) If the adjudication rule turns out to admit candidate-limited fact-check-matching counts, the row to create would be: Brazil, WhatsApp, May-October 2018, CONTENT, 0.85%, 100/11,700 unique transcribed audios, ground_truth=fact_checker (six Brazilian fact-checking agencies), classification_level=claim_level, denom_scope=political_news or topical, sampling_frame=convenience (publicly accessible politically-oriented groups), topic=politics_elections, confidence low.

rob.design: Non-probability corpus of WhatsApp messages, re-used from Resende et al. Frame: publicly accessible, politically-oriented WhatsApp groups in Brazil joined via invitation links posted on public websites; messages collected 21 May - 28 October 2018, spanning the national truck drivers' strike (21 May - 2 June) and the general election campaign (16 August - 28 October). Audio subset: 42,869 audio messages from 8,056 users across 364 groups; near-duplicates grouped by Chromaprint acoustic fingerprint above a manually chosen similarity threshold, giving 16,503 unique audios; Google Speech-to-Text transcription retained only where confidence exceeded 0.8 and the language was Portuguese, leaving 11,700 unique transcribed audios (about 71%). Misinformation identification: transcriptions were lemmatised, stopword-filtered, TF-IDF vectorised and cosine-compared against a database of claims checked as false by six Brazilian fact-checking agencies; the 300 highest-similarity pairs were manually reviewed and 100 confirmed as carrying the same content as the matched false claim; all remaining audios were labelled 'unchecked' rather than true. No inter-rater reliability reported for the manual review, and no random-sample validation of the unchecked set. Supplementary qualitative work: three semi-structured interviews and an online survey with 25 volunteers rating a random sample of 100 audios (50 misinformation, 50 unchecked), 3 raters per audio; the authors note the interviewees were familiar with misinformation research, a stated bias.
rob.item6_quote: We identified audios with misinformation by comparing each audio transcription in our dataset with a fact-checked claim marked as containing misinformation by at least one of the fact-checking agencies.
rob.item10_quote: As per the manual analysis, we found that only 100 out of the 300 transcriptions analyzed indeed carried the same content as the claim they were matched to with the highest similarity. These audios were marked as containing misinformation, and are the focus of our analyses in the following sections. All other 200 audio messages, as well as all other audios with lower similarity compared to the collected claims, were marked as unchecked.
